newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Giscard says no problem with mark-french rate.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Giscard says no problem with mark-french rate.

text.p: Former French President Valery Giscard d'Estaing said on Thursday in Bonn he was not calling for a devaluation of the French franc against the mark but added a stronger dollar would be useful for France's economy.

"The link between the franc and the mark is no problem," he said, adding the problem was the relation between the franc and the dollar. He would prefer to see the dollar at a rate of 5.5 francs per dollar from around 5.0 currently.

Speaking to a group of journalists after talks with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Giscard d'Estaing said he had not been advocating a depreciation of the franc against the mark in a French magazine article on Wednesday.
"Currencies (in the EMU) do not have a fixed parity," he said. "They are floating and only obliged to stay within the 15 percent band."

Giscard d'Estaing had called in a magazine article for a sharp depreciation in the franc against the dollar, implying a similar big fall against the mark, to revive growth and employment. His comments have slightly weakened the franc against the mark.

"The dollar at 5.5 French francs would be better and would enable the French economy to go back to growth and employment," he said in Bonn after a 75-minute meeting with Kohl that he described as "warm and friendly."
The former president, who meets Kohl from time to time, said he remained firmly committed to monetary union.
"I am taking a stand because I am very attached to good ties between France and Germany and to monetary union," he said.
Giscard d'Estaing also said that monetary union needed to be straightforward to succeed, which is why he suggested that the euro be fixed at a rate of seven French francs.
"Monetary union must be simple if we want it to be understood by the population," he said.
Earlier on Thursday in a brief telephone conversation, Kohl and French Prime Minister Alain Juppe made a point of repeating their determination to launch a single European currency in 1999.

"They reaffirmed the commitment of France and Germany to launch Economic and Monetary Union within the timetable and convergence criteria fixed by the (Maastricht) treaty," an official statement, released in both Paris and Bonn, said.
